overview:
Moses and Israel sing to the LORD for the victory at the sea. The song praises him as a warrior who threw horse and rider into the sea, mocks the enemy's boast, asks who among the gods is like him, and looks ahead: the nations of Canaan will freeze in fear as Israel passes, until God plants his people on his own mountain and reigns for ever. Miriam the prophetess leads the women with timbrels and dancing, singing the first line back. Then the march goes on into the wilderness of Shur: three days without water, bitter water at Marah made sweet by a tree, and rest at Elim with twelve wells and seventy palm trees.

Within a few verses Israel goes from singing to murmuring. Three days after the sea, the people who believed (14:31) ask, “What shall we drink?” (v. 24). Marah opens the wilderness pattern of need, complaint, and provision.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Verse 1 gives the song to Moses and the children of Israel, and v. 21 gives its refrain to Miriam. Tradition credits Moses with the book; many scholars see the song as an older poem set into the narrative.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Tradition places the song at the event. Many scholars count it among the oldest Hebrew poetry, perhaps 12th–10th century BC, because of its archaic grammar; the surrounding prose may be later.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Days after the Passover: about 1446 BC by 1 Kings 6:1, or the 13th century BC in many scholars' view.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Archaic Hebrew poetry (vv. 1–18, 21), with prose in vv. 19–20 and 22–27.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The shore of the sea, then the wilderness of Shur east of Egypt: Marah, three days on, and the oasis of Elim (vv. 22–27).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 14 tells the same events in prose; compare Psalms 78:13; 106:9–12. Alma 36:28 and Revelation 15:3 take up the song.

hermeneutics:
In the Baal myths from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), the storm god Baal defeats Yam, the Sea; then a palace is built for him on his mountain, Zaphon, and he is proclaimed king. The Song of the Sea moves in the same order: victory at the sea (vv. 1–12), the march to God's mountain and sanctuary (vv. 13–17), and the shout, “The LORD shall reign for ever and ever” (v. 18). The difference is pointed. The sea here is no rival god; it is water that God's breath piles up and lets fall (vv. 8, 10), and the enemy is Pharaoh. The question “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?” (v. 11) is asked in a world that told the other story.

When an army came home victorious, Israel's women went out to meet it with hand drums, dancing and singing short refrains back and forth, as they did for Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6–7) and as Jephthah's daughter did (Judges 11:34). Clay figurines of women holding frame drums are common finds in Iron Age Israel and Phoenicia. Miriam's part (vv. 20–21) is that familiar role: she leads the women out and answers with the song's opening couplet. Here the returning warrior is the LORD himself, and the army never fought.

structure.summary: An opening hymn, three stanzas that each close on a simile of sinking or stillness, and a closing acclamation (a common scholarly division). Not a chiasm.

rows.text: Opening hymn: “I will sing unto the LORD”
Stanza three ends: “as still as a stone”
Close: the sanctuary; “The LORD shall reign”

notes: **Similes:** the enemy sinks “as a stone” (v. 5) and “as lead” (v. 10); then the nations of Canaan stand “still as a stone” (v. 16) while Israel passes. The same image moves from the drowned to the terrified.
**The name:** the LORD (*YHWH*) is named ten times in vv. 1–18, and v. 3 stops to say “the LORD is his name.” “Thy right hand” comes twice in v. 6 and again in v. 12.
**Frame:** Miriam's couplet (v. 21) repeats the opening line (v. 1), so her refrain brackets the whole song.

Verse 21 ends the deliverance from Egypt (1:1–15:21), closing with Miriam's couplet. Verse 22 begins the journey to Sinai (15:22–18:27). Marah opens a run of wilderness crises: bitter water here, then hunger (ch. 16), thirst at Rephidim (17:1–7), and war with Amalek (17:8–16).

**Forward:** “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (v. 26) names God by a promise. In Revelation the victors stand by a sea of glass and sing “the song of Moses” and the song of the Lamb (Revelation 15:2–3).

traditions.text: Telling his son Helaman of his conversion, Alma ends in the song's terms: he will praise God for ever, for God brought the fathers out of Egypt and “swallowed up the Egyptians in the Red Sea.” Like Moses, he sets his own deliverance beside Israel's.

This revelation on priesthood ends with a new song that the redeemed will sing together in the last days: the Lord has brought again Zion and redeemed his people Israel. Like Moses' song it celebrates a redemption already worked and ends on God's glory “forever and ever.”

Philo pictures two choirs on the shore, the men led by Moses and the women by Miriam, singing hymns of thanks to God the Saviour. He says the Therapeutae, a contemplative Jewish community in Egypt, ended their festal nights by joining their men's and women's choirs into one, “an imitation of that one” at the Red Sea, and sang until sunrise.
traditions.cite: On the Life of Moses 1.180; On the Contemplative Life 85–89

traditions.text: Says the Hebrews spent the whole night after the crossing in hymns and rejoicing, and that Moses composed his song of praise in hexameter verse, the meter of Homer. For his Greek readers the song becomes a classical ode, and Moses something like a Greek poet.

After the crossing, Wisdom says, the righteous praised God with one accord, for wisdom “opened the mouth of the dumb” and made the tongues of infants eloquent. The Talmud tells the same scene in detail: babies on their mothers' laps and infants at the breast saw the divine presence and sang the words of v. 2, This is my God.

Rabbi Akiva reads the extra word “saying” in v. 1 to mean that the people answered Moses after each line with the refrain “I will sing unto the LORD,” as in reciting the Hallel psalms. Rabbi Nehemiah holds that they sang it together with him, as the Shema is recited.
Rabbi Meir notices that the Hebrew verb of v. 1 can be read “then Moses will sing.” He takes the future tense as proof from the Torah that the dead will rise, so that Moses will sing this song again.

Says that a maidservant at the sea saw what Ezekiel and the other prophets never saw, so plainly was God revealed that anyone could point and say, “This is my God” (v. 2). The Mekhilta also counts ten songs in Scripture, from the night in Egypt to the new song of the age to come, and places this one second.

The Hebrew behind the KJV's “prepare him an habitation” (v. 2) is a rare word that most translations render as glorify. One teaching reads it as a call to beautify the commandments: a fine sukkah, a fine Torah scroll. Abba Shaul splits the word into “I and he”: be like God, compassionate as he is compassionate.

The Mekhilta asks what tree healed Marah's water and lists answers from a willow to an olive, the bitterest of trees, to a cedar; Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel notes that God heals bitter with bitter. It reads the statute and ordinance of v. 25 as the Sabbath and honoring parents. The Talmud counts Marah as the place where Israel received ten commandments before Sinai.

In Ezekiel's Greek drama of the Exodus a scout reports Elim to Moses: a shady meadow by a stream, twelve springs pouring from a single rock, and seventy tall palms laden with fruit. He then describes a bird larger than an eagle, with a purple breast and golden neck, that all other birds follow, a creature often identified as the phoenix.

John sees those who have overcome the beast standing by a sea of glass mingled with fire and singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. The victory at the Red Sea becomes the pattern for the final victory of God's people.

Justin lists the tree Moses cast into Marah's bitter water among the figures of the cross, alongside the rod that divided the sea and the tree of life in paradise. Ambrose applies it to baptism: water without the preaching of the cross is of no avail, but when the cross is proclaimed over the font, the water is made sweet for grace. Tertullian had already said that the tree of Moses was Christ (On Baptism 9).
